parts.text: The song opens with a woman’s longing for her beloved’s kisses and delight in his love and name. She speaks to Jerusalem’s daughters about her beauty and sun-darkened appearance, explaining that her brothers made her tend vineyards while her own was neglected. She asks where her beloved feeds his flock so she need not wander uncertainly among other shepherds.

An exchange of admiration follows through images of ornaments, fragrant spices, a cluster from En-gedi, and dove-like eyes. The beloveds celebrate one another’s beauty and the pleasant setting of their shared love. Cedar, fir, greenery, and perfume give the opening chapter its language of richness and delight.

The lovers compare one another to flowers and a fruitful tree that gives refreshing shade. The woman describes being brought to a banqueting house beneath a banner of love and held in an affectionate embrace. Overwhelmed with desire, she asks support and charges Jerusalem’s daughters, ‘stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.’

She hears her beloved approaching like a swift deer over the hills. He calls her to arise and come away because winter has passed, flowers appear, birds sing, and vines blossom. A plea concerns little foxes spoiling the vineyards. She affirms their mutual belonging and calls him to return like a roe upon the mountains.

chapters.title: A night search and Solomon’s wedding procession

parts.text: On her bed at night, the woman seeks the one she loves but cannot find him. She rises to search the city’s streets and questions its watchmen. Soon afterward she finds him, holds him, and brings him toward her mother’s house. She again charges Jerusalem’s daughters, ‘stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.’

The scene turns to an impressive procession emerging from the wilderness with fragrant smoke. Solomon’s conveyance is surrounded by sixty armed men prepared against nighttime danger. Its materials include silver, gold, purple, and costly wood. The daughters of Zion are invited to see Solomon wearing the crown his mother gave him on his wedding day.

The man describes his beloved’s beauty through a sequence of comparisons: dove-like eyes, hair like goats on Gilead, teeth like washed sheep, scarlet lips, and a neck like David’s tower. Her breasts are compared to twin young roes. He declares her wholly beautiful and speaks of going to the mountain of myrrh and hill of frankincense.

Calling her his sister and spouse, he invites her from Lebanon and praises love sweeter than wine. She is compared to an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain, and an orchard filled with fragrant plants and flowing water. The woman calls upon the winds to carry the garden’s perfume and invites her beloved to enjoy its fruit.

chapters.title: The beloved withdraws and is sought again

parts.text: The man announces his arrival in the garden and enjoyment of its fruits. The woman then describes sleeping while her heart wakes and hearing her beloved knock. She hesitates, but rises to open after he reaches toward the door. He has gone, and her search brings no answer. The watchmen wound her and remove her veil. She asks Jerusalem’s daughters to tell him she is sick with love.

When they ask what distinguishes him from others, she answers with an elaborate portrait of beauty and strength, using gold, spices, precious stones, ivory, and Lebanon. She concludes that he is altogether lovely: both her beloved and her friend.

The daughters of Jerusalem ask where the beloved has gone so they may seek him with the woman. She answers that he is in his garden among spices and lilies, and reaffirms their mutual belonging. The language restores attention to the relationship after the preceding search.

The man praises her as beautiful as Tirzah and Jerusalem and as striking as an army with banners. Her beauty overwhelms him, and she is uniquely cherished among queens, concubines, and maidens. Garden imagery returns as the speaker goes to see new growth. The chapter closes with a call for the Shulamite to return so others may look upon her.

chapters.title: Delight and an invitation to the vineyards

parts.text: The beloved woman’s beauty is celebrated from her sandaled feet upward through comparisons to skillful workmanship, ivory, pools, towers, fruit, and a palm tree. The speech expresses attraction, admiration, and a desire for closeness. Her mouth is compared to the finest wine.

The woman declares that she belongs to her beloved and that his desire is toward her. She invites him to go into the fields, stay in the villages, and rise early to examine the vineyards and budding fruit. Amid fragrant mandrakes and stored delicacies, she promises to give him her love.

chapters.title: Love that cannot be purchased or quenched

parts.text: The woman longs to express affection openly and bring her beloved into her mother’s house. The familiar charge returns: ‘stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.’ A figure comes from the wilderness leaning upon her beloved, and love is described as strong as death, with a fierce flame. Many waters cannot quench it, and no amount of wealth can buy it.

Discussion turns to a younger sister’s maturity and protection, followed by the woman’s affirmation of her own readiness and peace. Solomon’s vineyard is contrasted with the vineyard she regards as her own. Companions wish to hear her voice, and the song closes with her call for the beloved to hurry like a roe or young hart over fragrant mountains.
